articles.title: Optimizing Performance at Scotiabank
articles.summary: How I reduced load times by 40% in the Scotiabank Peru iOS app through lazy loading, image caching, and optimized network calls.
articles.content:
When I joined the Scotiabank project, the app's main dashboard took over 3 seconds to load. Users were frustrated, and the metrics showed a 15% drop-off rate.

## The Problem

The dashboard was loading all data synchronously — account balances, recent transactions, promotions, and notifications — all in a single blocking call.

## The Solution

**1. Lazy Loading**: I broke the monolithic API call into independent modules that load in parallel. The account balance (critical) loads first, while transactions and promotions load asynchronously.

**2. Image Caching**: Promotional banners were being re-downloaded every session. I implemented a disk cache with NSCache that reduced bandwidth by 60%.

**3. Prefetching**: Using URLSession's prefetch API, the app starts loading the next screen's data before the user navigates.

## Results

- Load time: 3.2s → 1.1s (65% reduction)
- Crash rate: -40%
- User retention: +12% in the first month

The key lesson: performance optimization isn't about clever algorithms — it's about understanding user behavior and loading what matters first.

articles.title: VIPER vs MVVM in Practice
articles.summary: After using both patterns extensively in production, here's my honest take on when to use each one.
articles.content:
I've built production apps with both VIPER and MVVM. Here's what I've learned.

## MVVM: When to Use It

MVVM shines in small to medium apps. The ViewModel handles business logic and the View observes changes. It's simple, testable, and most iOS developers understand it.

**Pros:**
- Fast to implement
- Easy to test ViewModels
- Works great with Combine/RxSwift
- Low boilerplate

**Cons:**
- ViewModels can become massive (Massive ViewModel problem)
- Navigation logic gets messy
- Hard to enforce boundaries in large teams

## VIPER: When to Use It

VIPER is built for scale. Each module has clear responsibilities: View, Interactor, Presenter, Entity, Router.

**Pros:**
- Crystal clear separation of concerns
- Each component is independently testable
- Router handles navigation cleanly
- Perfect for large teams — everyone knows where code goes

**Cons:**
- Significant boilerplate
- Overkill for simple screens
- Learning curve for new developers

## My Rule of Thumb

- Solo/small team, < 20 screens → MVVM
- Large team, > 20 screens, banking/enterprise → VIPER
- Mixed: use VIPER for complex modules, MVVM for simple ones

The architecture should serve the team, not the other way around.

articles.title: Unit Testing: The Investment That Pays Off
articles.summary: Why I push for 80%+ test coverage and how it saved us from 3 critical production bugs at Scotiabank.
articles.content:
When I proposed increasing test coverage from 30% to 80% at Scotiabank, the team pushed back. 'We don't have time for tests.' Here's how I convinced them.

## The Cost of No Tests

In Q1 2023, we had 3 critical production bugs:

1. **Currency formatting bug** — amounts displayed without decimals for Chilean peso transactions
2. **Session expiry race condition** — users could initiate transfers with expired tokens
3. **Cache invalidation** — stale account balances shown after transfers

All three would have been caught by basic unit tests.

## The Approach

I didn't ask for permission to stop feature work. Instead:

1. **Test alongside features** — every new PR required tests for the new code
2. **Test the scary parts first** — payment processing, authentication, data mapping
3. **Automate on CI** — tests run on every PR, coverage gate at 80%

## The Payoff

After 6 months:
- Coverage: 32% → 84%
- Production bugs: -60%
- Developer confidence: immeasurable
- Onboarding time: -30% (tests as documentation)

The best test is the one that catches a bug before your users do.

articles.title: From React Native to Swift: Why I Switched
articles.summary: My journey from cross-platform to native iOS development, and why I never looked back.
articles.content:
I started my mobile career with React Native. I built maps, real-time features, and interactive UIs with JavaScript. It was fast, productive, and the hot reload was addictive.

## Why I Switched

**Performance ceiling**: For the healthcare apps I was building (ehCOS Remote Health), React Native's bridge was a bottleneck. Medical device integration required native modules anyway.

**Platform depth**: iOS has incredible APIs — HealthKit, Core Bluetooth, ARKit — that React Native wraps poorly or not at all.

**Career trajectory**: The highest-paying iOS roles require deep platform knowledge. React Native developers are more replaceable.

## What I Kept

React Native taught me:
- Component-based thinking (applies to SwiftUI)
- State management patterns (applies to Combine)
- Fast iteration mindset

## The Verdict

React Native is great for MVPs and content-driven apps. But if you're building banking apps, healthcare systems, or anything that needs to feel truly native — go native.

I don't regret the React Native years. They made me a better iOS developer.

articles.title: Building Digital Wallet Interoperability at Scotiabank
articles.summary: How I implemented cross-wallet P2P transfers at Scotiabank Peru, enabling interoperability across 20+ financial institutions with QR standards and strict security protocols.
articles.content:
I led the implementation of digital wallet interoperability at Scotiabank Peru — a feature that allows P2P transfers between 20+ banks and digital wallets using QR codes, regulated by the SBS (banking regulator).

## The Challenge

Making transfers seamless across institutions with different systems, APIs, and security standards. The user scans a QR or enters a phone number, and money moves between any participating wallet — Scotiabank, BCP, Interbank, BBVA, Yape, Plin, and more.

## The Biggest Problem: Data Exposure

During initial testing, we discovered a critical privacy issue. When a user entered a phone number to transfer money, the API returned the recipient's **full legal name**. Users quickly figured this out and started using the transfer flow as a lookup tool — enter any phone number, get someone's full name.

This was a serious privacy vulnerability. We worked with the backend team to implement:
- **Name masking**: Only showing partial names (e.g., "J*** Pérez G***")
- **Rate limiting**: Limiting lookup attempts per user per hour
- **Behavioral monitoring**: Flagging accounts that queried names without completing transfers

## Security at Every Step

Every feature went through rigorous security review. Some examples:
- QR code validation to prevent tampered codes from redirecting funds
- Transaction signing to ensure amounts couldn't be modified in transit
- Session validation at each step of the transfer flow
- Biometric confirmation before executing transfers

## Help Center Integration

We also built an in-app help center (promoted by SBS regulation) that guides users step by step through the interoperability process — with visual tutorials, FAQs, and direct support channels.

## Impact

This feature put Scotiabank Peru on the interoperability map, enabling users to send and receive money across the entire Peruvian financial ecosystem without leaving the app. The key lesson: in banking, security isn't a feature — it's the foundation.

articles.title: Killing Singletons: Migrating to Dependency Injection
articles.summary: How I'm leading the migration from singleton-heavy MVVM to protocol-based dependency injection at Scotiabank, improving testability and reducing coupling.
articles.content:
The Scotiabank Peru iOS app was built with MVVM — but a limited version. ViewModels accessed services through singletons, making unit testing nearly impossible and creating hidden dependencies everywhere.

## The Problem with Singletons

Singletons seem convenient until you need to:
- **Test in isolation**: You can't mock a singleton without swizzling or global state hacks
- **Understand dependencies**: A ViewModel that calls `NetworkManager.shared` gives you no clue what it actually needs
- **Run tests in parallel**: Shared mutable state between tests causes flaky results

## The Migration Strategy

I didn't propose a big-bang rewrite. Instead:

**1. Protocol-first**: Every service gets a protocol. `NetworkManager` becomes `NetworkManaging`. The concrete class conforms, but consumers only know the protocol.

**2. Constructor injection**: ViewModels receive their dependencies through init. No more `.shared` calls inside business logic.

**3. DI Container**: A centralized container registers and resolves dependencies. Singletons still exist at the container level, but the rest of the code doesn't know or care.

**4. Incremental adoption**: New features use DI from day one. Existing features migrate when they're touched for bug fixes or enhancements.

## Reducing Legacy Dependencies

Alongside the DI migration, I reduced third-party library dependencies by 90%. Many were legacy libraries that had native replacements in modern iOS — URLSession instead of custom networking wrappers, Codable instead of manual JSON parsing, async/await instead of callback-based libraries.

## Hunting Circular References

With the codebase under a microscope, I also audited for retain cycles using Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger. Found several circular references between ViewModels and their closures, coordinators holding strong references to child coordinators, and delegate patterns missing `weak` declarations. Each fix reduced the app's memory footprint.

## The Result

The app is progressively becoming more testable, more maintainable, and lighter. The team is writing tests for features that were previously untestable. The architecture is evolving without breaking anything in production.

The lesson: you don't need permission to improve architecture. Just make every PR slightly better than what was there before.

articles.title: Security Lessons from Banking App Development
articles.summary: Real security challenges I've faced building banking apps — from certificate pinning to data exposure, and the mindset shift required for financial software.
articles.content:
After years building banking apps, I've learned that security in mobile development isn't about adding a library — it's about thinking differently at every layer.

## Certificate Pinning: Trust No One

In a banking app, you can't trust the network. Man-in-the-middle attacks are real, especially on public Wi-Fi. We implement certificate pinning with per-host evaluation — each API endpoint is validated against pinned certificates bundled in the app.

The tricky part: certificate rotation. If the server updates its certificate and you haven't pushed an app update with the new pin, your users are locked out. We maintain a fallback evaluation chain and coordinate certificate rotations with the backend team weeks in advance.

## The Privacy Trap

The interoperability feature taught us a hard lesson: **any data you return to the client can be abused**. We returned full recipient names for transfer confirmation, and users turned it into a name-lookup service. Now every piece of data goes through a privacy review: "What's the minimum the user needs to see?"

## Biometric Authentication Done Right

FaceID/TouchID seem simple, but in banking:
- You need a fallback (PIN) for when biometrics fail
- You must handle device biometric changes (new face enrolled = re-authenticate)
- Session tokens must be stored in the Secure Enclave, not just Keychain
- You need to distinguish between app-level auth and transaction-level auth

## Secure Storage Layers

Not everything goes in the Keychain. We use a tiered approach:
- **Keychain** (Secure Enclave): Authentication tokens, biometric keys
- **Encrypted UserDefaults**: User preferences, non-sensitive settings
- **Memory only**: Transaction data, session state (never persisted)

## The Mindset Shift

In consumer apps, you optimize for speed and UX. In banking, you optimize for **correctness and auditability**. Every API call is logged. Every state transition is validated. Every error is a potential security event.

The most important security tool isn't a library — it's the question: "What happens if someone malicious uses this feature?"
